name: Fire
miniText: How does habitat connectivity determine whether a spreading disturbance crosses a landscape? NetLogo Fire initializes randomly occupied tree patches and ignites the left boundary. Burning trees ignite their four orthogonal neighbors; empty patches interrupt transmission. Broadbent and Hammersley provide the random-medium framework for interpreting connected paths [1], while Grassberger relates epidemic propagation to dynamical percolation [2]. The simulation illustrates a sharp connectivity-dependent change in crossing probability, with finite landscapes and random realizations producing variable outcomes. It assumes no wind, spotting, fuel variation or regrowth. Drossel and Schwabl supply a useful contrast: their forest-fire model adds growth and lightning and investigates self-organized criticality [3]. Those mechanisms are absent from this baseline, so its density-controlled transition does not by itself demonstrate self-organization or validate predictions for actual wildfires.

Registrant abstract consulted: ABSTRACT The paper studies, in a general way, how the random properties of a ‘medium’ influence the percolation of a ‘fluid’ through it. The treatment diifers from conventional diffusion theory, in which it is the random properties of the fluid that matter. Fluid and medium bear general interpretations: for example, solute diffusing through solvent, electrons migrating over an atomic lattice, molecules penetrating a porous solid, disease infecting a community, etc.
